clinician.final_diagnosis: Type II hereditary antithrombin III deficiency (ATD) in a 25-year-old male and his father, with associated patent foramen ovale and white matter lesions
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 25-year-old previously healthy male presented with a 4+ year history of recurrent bilateral paroxysmal headaches (predominantly afternoon onset, 1-2 hour duration, spontaneously relieved by rest) and occasional emotional-triggered limb numbness. Physical examination was negative. Laboratory workup revealed decreased antithrombin III activity (72.2%, reference 80-120%) with normal AT III antigen level (235 mg/L, reference 180-392 mg/L), consistent with type II AT III deficiency. Whole exon sequencing identified a novel heterozygous missense mutation in the SERPINC1 gene (1q25.1), confirmed by Sanger sequencing in the father. Brain MRI showed multiple discrete hyperintense white matter lesions in periventricular, deep white matter, frontal, and parietal regions bilaterally, distributed perpendicular to lateral ventricles with some confluent lesions, non-enhancing on T1-weighted contrast imaging. CSF analysis was negative for oligoclonal bands with normal IgG index, ruling out demyelinating disease. Cardiac evaluation by transcranial doppler and transthoracic echocardiography identified patent foramen ovale, identified as the most likely reason for the patient's migraine. The patient underwent percutaneous PFO closure surgery and received oral antiplatelet therapy. At 1 and 6 month follow-up, the patient reported significant improvement in headache pain degree, attack frequency, and duration, while MRI lesions remained unchanged. The father was found to have the same SERPINC1 mutation with similarly decreased AT III activity (75.1%) and normal antigen level (263.3 mg/L), with multiple asymptomatic white matter lesions on MRI, confirming the hereditary nature of type II AT III deficiency.
